limits: Integer coding suits trees and not linear models, so the ridge rows are references only.
Only thirty splits, so power is lower than in the ridge rounds.
Retrospective; no mechanism, clinical or drug-choice claim; no meta-learning or RSI.

what_survives_and_what_must_be_narrowed.survives: the algebraic fact: each drug maps to exactly one pathway level, so the pathway one-hots are a linear transform of the drug one-hots and for a linear model they span no new directions. Ridge reproduces the exact zero (-0.0000).
what_survives_and_what_must_be_narrowed.must_be_narrowed: the functional claim 'substitute, never complement' holds only for linear models. Under gradient boosting the coarsening adds +0.0152 in rank correlation [0.0146, 0.0159], fifteen times the minimum detectable effect of 0.0010.
what_survives_and_what_must_be_narrowed.corrected_statement: pathway carries no additional INFORMATION, but its coarser granularity is a useful inductive bias for a nonlinear model: it offers splits that generalise across drugs.

why_boosting_can_use_it.ridge: adding a linear transform of existing columns cannot change the column space, so the fit is unchanged
why_boosting_can_use_it.boosting: the same information presented at a coarser granularity enables different splits. A tree that splits on pathway generalises across all drugs in that pathway, which a split on drug identity cannot do. So the gain comes from inductive bias, not from information.
why_boosting_can_use_it.consequence: redundant features can still help nonlinear models, and 'no new information' does not imply 'no use'

how_big.comparison_to_the_seen_pools: the same order as the +0.020 and +0.025 rank gains found when one drug was seen (C103)
how_big.reading: small, but it is the same size as the substitute effect in the partially-informed regime, which puts it on the same footing rather than dismissing it
